title: Maximum Profit from Valid Topological Order in DAG
statement:
You get a directed acyclic graph with `n` nodes labeled `0` to `n - 1`. Each `edges[i] = [u, v]` is an edge from `u` to `v`, and node `i` carries the value `score[i]`.

Arrange all `n` nodes in a topological order: a sequence in which, for every edge `[u, v]`, node `u` appears earlier than node `v`. Positions are counted from 1, and node `i` placed at position `p` earns `score[i] * p`. The profit of an order is the total earned by all its nodes. Return the largest profit that any topological order achieves.
constraints: edges[i] == [u, v] is a directed edge from u to v
signature: int maxProfit(int n, int[][] edges, int[] score)
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every topological order works but can mean `n!` orders. Once some set of nodes fills the first positions, the next node takes position (size of the set) + 1, and which nodes may go next depends only on which nodes are placed, not on their order. So the best profit for "these nodes come first" depends on the set alone, and with `n <= 22` a set fits in a bitmask: at most 2^22 states.

## Approach

1. Build `before[node]`, the bitmask of nodes that have an edge into `node`.
2. `dp[mask]` is the best profit when exactly the nodes in `mask` occupy positions 1 to |mask|. Set `dp[0] = 0` and the rest to `-1` (not reachable).
3. Visit masks in increasing order: adding a node makes a mask larger, so each state is final before it is extended. Skip masks at `-1`.
4. Count the bits of `mask` to get `position`, the slot the next node takes.
5. For each `node` not in `mask` whose `before[node]` lies entirely inside `mask`, update `dp[mask | 1 << node]` with `dp[mask] + score[node] * position`.
6. Return `dp[full]`, the state with every node placed.

## Example 1, step by step

`edges = [[0,1]]`, `score = [2,3]`, so `before = [0, 1]`.

- `mask = 0`: `position = 1`. Node 0 has no parents: `dp[1] = 0 + 2·1 = 2`. Node 1 still needs node 0.
- `mask = 1` (node 0 placed): `position = 2`. Node 1 is allowed now: `dp[3] = 2 + 3·2 = 8`.
- `mask = 2` stays `-1`: node 1 can never come first.

The answer is `dp[3] = 8`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(2^n · n): each mask counts its bits and tries every node once.
- Space: O(2^n) for `dp`.

## Pitfalls

- Placing the smallest available score first is not optimal: with the edge `0 → 1` and `score = [5, 1, 4]` it builds 2, 0, 1 for 17, but 0, 1, 2 earns 19 (Test 3).
- A node may go next only when **all** its parents are placed: compare `before[node] & mask` with the whole `before[node]`.
- Starting every state at `0` instead of `-1` lets the DP extend sets no valid order produces; in Test 4 it would place node 2 after its own children and report 300 instead of 105.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `before[node]` | bitmask of the nodes with an edge into `node` |
| `full` | mask with all `n` nodes placed |
| `dp[mask]` | best profit with exactly `mask` in the first positions, or `-1` |
| `mask` | the set of nodes already placed |
| `position` | 1-based position the next node takes |
| `rest` | `mask` with its bits cleared one at a time while counting |
| `node`, `placed` | candidate for the next position, and whether it is already in `mask` |
| `next` | the set after placing `node` |
